chapters.title: The Editor to the Reader
paragraphs: It pains us deeply that we lack first-hand testimony for the last remarkable days of our friend, so that we must break off his letters here and fill the gap with a connected account.

I felt it my duty to gather what I could from the lips of people who knew his story well. It is a simple one, and all the reports agree, except in a few small details; only on the characters of those involved do opinions and judgments differ.

There is nothing left for us but to set down conscientiously what our repeated efforts have let us learn, to insert the letters the dead man left behind, and not to overlook the smallest scrap from his hand — especially since it is so hard to uncover the true, particular motives of even a single action when it occurs among people who are not of the common run.

Ill-humor and discontent had struck ever deeper roots in Werther's soul and grown so entangled together that they took over his whole being. The harmony of his mind was wholly destroyed; an inner heat and violence, which threw all his natural powers into disorder, had the unhappiest effects on him, and left him at last so worn out that he struggled up against it more painfully than he had ever fought his other troubles. The anguish of his heart ate away the rest of his powers of mind, his liveliness, his quick wit; he became a wretched companion, ever unhappier and, the unhappier he grew, the more unjust. So at least Albert's friends say. They claim, too, that Werther couldn't rightly judge Albert, that pure, calm man who had now come into a happiness he'd long wished for, and who wanted to keep it — whereas Werther, day by day, was as it were spending up his whole fortune only to suffer the more bitterly each evening. Albert hadn't changed in so short a time; he was still the same man Werther had known from the start, had so prized and honored. He loved Charlotte above all things, was proud of her, and wanted her seen by everyone as the most glorious of creatures. Can we blame him, then, for wanting to turn away even the shadow of suspicion, for being unwilling in that moment to share his precious prize with anyone, even in the most innocent way? We grant that Albert often left his wife's room when Werther was with her — but not out of hate or dislike of his friend, only because he felt Werther was oppressed by his presence.
Charlotte's father, kept indoors by an illness, sent his carriage for her, and she drove out. It was a fine winter day; the first heavy snow had fallen and lay over the whole country.
Werther went out the next morning to fetch Charlotte home, in case Albert wasn't there to walk her back.

The clear weather could do little for his clouded spirit; a dull weight pressed on his soul, gloomy pictures had settled in him, and his mind knew no movement but from one painful thought to the next.

As he lived now in eternal discord with himself, the state of others seemed to him only more troubled and confused; he believed he'd upset the fine balance between Albert and his wife, and reproached himself for it, mixed with a secret resentment against the husband.

On the way his thoughts ran on this too. "Yes, yes," he said to himself, grinding his teeth, "so this is the close, confiding, tender, all-sharing friendship, the calm, lasting faithfulness! Sated comfort, that's all it is! Doesn't any wretched piece of business mean more to him than his dear, precious wife? Does he know how to value his luck? Does he honor her as she deserves? He has her — well, he has her; I know it, as I know other things too; I think I've grown used to the idea — it will drive me mad yet, it will be the death of me. And has his friendship for me held up? Doesn't he already see in my attachment to Charlotte a trespass on his rights, in my attentions to her a quiet reproach? I know it well, I feel it: he doesn't like to see me, he wishes me gone, my presence is a burden to him."

Often he'd check his hurried step, often stand still and seem about to turn back; yet again and again he bent his way forward, and so, with such thoughts and inner talk, came at last, half against his will, to the hunting-lodge.

He stepped into the doorway, asked after the old man and Charlotte, and found the house in some commotion. The eldest boy told him a dreadful thing had happened at Walheim — a peasant had been killed! It made no special impression on him. He went in and found Charlotte busy talking the old man out of going himself, ill as he was, to look into the matter on the spot. The murderer was still unknown; the dead man had been found that morning at his own door. There were guesses: the victim had been a widow's hired man, who'd had another in the place before him, one who'd been turned out of the house with bad feeling.

When Werther heard this he started up violently. "Can it be!" he cried. "I must go out there — I can't stay a moment." He hurried toward Walheim; every memory came alive in him, and he didn't doubt for an instant that the deed had been done by the man he'd talked with so often, the man he'd grown so fond of. As he had to pass under the lindens to reach the inn where the body had been carried, the once so-loved spot horrified him. The threshold where the neighbors' children had so often played was fouled with blood. Love and faithfulness, the finest of human feelings, had turned to violence and murder. The great trees stood bare and frosted; the lovely hedges arching over the low churchyard wall had lost their leaves, and the gravestones, deep in snow, looked through the gaps.

As he came up to the inn, in front of which the whole village had gathered, a shouting broke out. From a distance a troop of armed men could be seen, and everyone cried that they were bringing in the murderer. Werther looked, and was not long in doubt. Yes — it was the hired man, so in love with the widow, the one he'd met a while back wandering about in that quiet rage, that hidden despair.

"What have you done, you wretched man?" Werther cried, going up to the prisoner. The man looked at him quietly, said nothing, and at last answered quite calmly: "No one will have her now, and she'll have no one." They took the prisoner into the inn, and Werther hurried away. That terrible, violent meeting had shaken everything loose in him. For a moment it tore him out of his gloom, his despondency, his dull resignation; an irresistible sympathy took hold of him, and an unspeakable longing to save the man. He felt him so unhappy, found him as a criminal so blameless, put himself so deep into the man's place, that he was sure he could bring others round to the same view. He was already burning to speak for him; already the most forceful defense crowded to his lips; he hurried to the lodge, and couldn't keep from half-aloud rehearsing, on the way, everything he meant to lay before the magistrate.

When he came in, he found Albert already there, which put him out of countenance for a moment; but he soon collected himself and pressed his views warmly on the magistrate. The man shook his head, and though Werther urged everything a man can urge to plead another's cause, with all the warmth, passion, and truth of it, the magistrate, as one may guess, was unmoved. On the contrary, he cut our friend's speech short, argued against him hotly, even scolded him for taking a murderer's side; he showed that on such a line every law would be undone, all the safety of the state destroyed; and added that in such a matter he could do nothing without taking on the heaviest responsibility — everything must take its ordered course, go the way it always goes.

Even then Werther didn't give it up; he only begged the magistrate to look the other way if someone helped the man to escape! That too was refused. Albert, who finally joined the talk, took the old man's side. Werther was outvoted, and went off in the most fearful pain, after the magistrate had said to him several times: "No, he can't be saved!"
How deep those words must have cut him, we can see from a little scrap found among his papers, surely written that same day:
"You cannot be saved, unhappy man! I see clearly that we cannot be saved."

What Albert had said about the prisoner's affair, there in front of the magistrate, had revolted Werther utterly; he thought he'd caught in it a touch of feeling against himself, and though, when he turned it over, it couldn't escape his sense that both men were right, still it seemed to him that to admit it, to grant it, would be to give up his own inmost self.
A note of his about this, touching his whole relation to Albert, has been found among his papers.
"What's the good of telling myself again and again that he's upright and good? It tears at my insides; I can't be just to him."

On a mild evening, with the weather turning to thaw, Charlotte and Albert were walking home together. Now and then she looked about her, as if she missed Werther's company. Albert began to speak of him, found fault with him, while still doing him justice; he touched on his unhappy passion and wished it were possible to send him away. "I wish it for our own sakes too," he said. "And I ask you," he went on, "to give his behavior toward you another turn, to have him come less often. People are noticing, and I know we've been talked of here and there." Charlotte said nothing, and Albert seemed to feel her silence; at least from then on he never mentioned Werther to her again, and when she spoke of him he let it drop or turned the talk elsewhere.

The vain attempt Werther had made to save the wretched man was the last flicker of a dying flame; from then on he sank only the deeper into pain and inaction; he was nearly beside himself when he heard he might be summoned to give witness against the man, who was now talking his way out of it.

Everything unpleasant that had ever met him in his active life — the vexation at the embassy, everything else that had failed and stung him — heaved up and down in his soul. He found in all this a kind of justification for doing nothing; he felt cut off from every prospect, unfit to lay hold of any handle on the ordinary business of life; and so, given over wholly to his strange feeling, his way of thinking, and an endless passion, in the eternal sameness of a sad keeping-company with the lovely, beloved woman whose peace he wrecked, working off his powers, driving them without aim or prospect, he came always nearer the mournful end.
A few letters he left behind are the strongest witnesses of his confusion and his passion, of his doing and striving, and of his weariness of life; we set them here.
December 12.

Dear Wilhelm, I'm in the state of those poor souls who were thought to be hounded by an evil spirit. Sometimes it seizes me — not fear, not dread, an inner, unknown raging that threatens to tear open my breast, that chokes my throat! Then I'm out and about in the fearful night-scenes of this hostile season.

Last evening I had to go out. A sudden thaw had set in; I'd heard the river had risen, all the streams were swollen, and my dear valley below Walheim was under water! At night, past eleven, I ran out. A fearful sight, to watch the swirling floods come roaring down from the cliffs in the moonlight — over fields and meadows and hedges, and the whole wide valley, up and down, one storming lake in the howling wind! And when the moon came out again and lay above the black clouds, and the flood rolled and crashed before me in its grand and awful glory, a shudder ran over me, and then a longing! Ah, with open arms I stood facing the gulf and breathed: down! down! and lost myself in the rapture of hurling my torments, my sufferings, down there — to roar away with the waves! Oh — and you couldn't lift your foot from the ground and make an end of all your pain! My hour isn't run out yet, I feel it. O Wilhelm, how gladly I'd have given up my human shape to tear the clouds apart with that wind, to take hold of the flood! Ha! and won't this prisoner have that joy granted him one day?

And as I looked down so wistfully at a spot where I'd rested with Charlotte under a willow on a hot walk — that too was drowned, and I could hardly tell where the willow was, Wilhelm! And her meadows, I thought, the country round her lodge! How battered our bower must be now by the raging torrent! And the sunbeam of the past shone in, the way a dream of pastures, meadows, and high office shines in on a prisoner. I stood there — I don't reproach myself, for I have the courage to die. — I would have — Now I sit here like an old woman who gleans her firewood from the fences and her bread from door to door, to draw out and ease a moment longer her fading, joyless life.
December 15.

What is it with me, dear Wilhelm? I'm afraid of myself! Isn't my love for her the holiest, purest, most brotherly love? Have I ever felt a guilty wish in my soul? — But I won't swear to it. — And now, dreams! Oh, how truly the people felt it who blamed such contrary forces on strange powers outside us! Tonight! — I tremble to say it — I held her in my arms, pressed tight to my breast, and covered her love-whispering mouth with endless kisses; my eye swam in the drunkenness of hers! God! am I guilty that even now I feel a bliss in calling back those white-hot joys with my whole heart? Charlotte! Charlotte! — And it's all over with me! My senses are tangled; for a week now I've had no power of thought, my eyes are full of tears. I'm nowhere well, and everywhere well. I wish for nothing, ask for nothing. It would be better for me to go.

Under such conditions the resolve to leave the world had, in Werther's soul, gained ever more force. Since his return to Charlotte it had always been his last prospect and hope; but he'd told himself it should be no hasty, no rash act — he wanted to take the step with the firmest conviction, in the calmest possible resolution.
His doubts, his struggle with himself, show in a note that seems to be the opening of a letter to Wilhelm, found undated among his papers:
"Her presence, her fate, her sympathy for mine, still wring the last tears out of my burnt-up brain.

"To lift the curtain and step behind it! That's all! And why the shrinking and dread? Because we don't know how it looks back there? Because there's no returning? And because it's the way of our mind to suppose confusion and darkness where we know nothing for certain."
At last he grew ever more familiar and friendly with the sad thought, and his resolve hardened and stood fast; the following ambiguous letter, written to his friend, is proof of it.
December 20.

I thank your love, Wilhelm, for taking up my word the way you did. Yes, you're right: it's better for me to go. Your proposal that I come back to you doesn't quite please me; at least I'd like to make a little round trip first, the more so as we can hope for a long frost and good roads. It's a great kindness, too, that you want to come and fetch me; only give it a fortnight, and wait for one more letter from me. Nothing should be plucked before it's ripe. And a fortnight more or less makes a great difference. Tell my mother she must pray for her son, and that I beg her pardon for all the trouble I've caused her. It was my fate to grieve those I owed joy. Farewell, dearest friend! Heaven's every blessing on you! Farewell!

What was going on in Charlotte's soul during this time, toward her husband, toward her unhappy friend, we can hardly put into words — though, knowing her nature, we can form some quiet idea of it, and a fine woman's soul can think its way into hers and feel with her.

This much is sure: she was firmly set on doing all she could to keep Werther away, and if she held back, it was out of a heartfelt, sparing friendship, because she knew how much it would cost him, knew it would be all but impossible. Yet in this stretch she was pressed harder to be in earnest; her husband kept wholly silent about the matter, as she did too — all the more reason for her to prove to him in act that her mind matched his.

The same day Werther wrote that last letter to his friend — it was the Sunday before Christmas — he came to Charlotte in the evening and found her alone. She was busy putting in order some toys she'd readied as Christmas gifts for her little brothers and sisters. He spoke of the joy the children would have, and of the times when a door flung suddenly open and the sight of a tree decked with candles, sweets, and apples sends you into a heaven of delight. "You," said Charlotte, hiding her unease behind a sweet smile, "you shall have a gift too, if you're good — a little wax taper and something more." "And what do you call being good?" he cried. "How am I to be? How can I be, dearest Charlotte?" "Thursday evening," she said, "is Christmas Eve; the children are coming, my father too; each gets his gift; come then as well — but not before." Werther was struck. "I beg you," she went on, "it must be so; I beg it for the sake of my peace; it can't go on, it can't." He turned his eyes from her, paced the room, and muttered between his teeth, "It can't go on!" Charlotte, feeling the dreadful state those words had put him in, tried to turn his thoughts with all sorts of questions, but in vain. "No, Charlotte," he cried, "I'll not see you again!" "Why so?" she answered. "Werther, you can, you must see us again — only govern yourself. Oh, why were you born with this violence, this clinging, unconquerable passion for everything you once take hold of? I beg you," she went on, taking his hand, "govern yourself! Your mind, your learning, your gifts — what manifold joys they could give you! Be a man; turn this sad attachment away from a creature who can do nothing but pity you." He ground his teeth and looked at her darkly. She kept his hand. "Just one quiet moment, Werther!" she said. "Don't you feel that you're deceiving yourself, throwing yourself away on purpose? Why me, Werther? Me, of all people, who belong to another? Why that? I fear, I fear it's only the impossibility of having me that makes this wish so charming to you." He drew his hand from hers, looking at her with a fixed, angry eye. "Wise!" he cried, "very wise! Did Albert make that remark, perhaps? Clever! very clever!" "Anyone might make it," she answered. "And in all the wide world is there no girl who could fill the wishes of your heart? Bring yourself to it, look for her, and I swear you'll find her. For a long time I've been afraid for you, and for us, at this narrowing-in you've shut yourself into. Bring yourself to it; a journey will, must, scatter all this. Look, find an object worthy of your love, and come back, and let us together taste the bliss of a true friendship."

"That," said Werther with a cold laugh, "should be printed and recommended to all tutors. Dear Charlotte! Give me a little peace yet, and all will be well." "Only this, Werther: don't come again before Christmas Eve!" He was about to answer when Albert came into the room. They wished each other a cold good evening and walked up and down the room side by side in some embarrassment. Werther started some trifling talk that soon ran dry; Albert did the same, then asked his wife about some errands, and hearing they weren't done, said a few words to her that struck Werther as cold, even hard. He wanted to go and couldn't, and lingered until eight, his ill-humor and resentment building, until the table was laid, and he took up his hat and stick. Albert asked him to stay; but Werther, taking it for an empty courtesy, thanked him coldly and went.

He came home, took the light from his boy's hand, and went alone to his room; he talked aloud to himself, weeping, walked about in a heat, and at last threw himself, dressed, on the bed, where his servant found him toward eleven when he ventured in to ask whether he should pull off his master's boots. Werther let him, and told him not to come in the morning until he rang.

On Monday morning, the twenty-first of December, he wrote Charlotte the following letter, found sealed on his desk after his death and brought to her; I set it in here piece by piece, as the circumstances show it was written.

It's decided, Charlotte, I will die, and I write this to you with no romantic high feeling, calmly, on the morning of the day I'll see you for the last time. By the time you read this, dearest, the cold grave will already cover the stiff remains of the restless, unhappy man who knows no sweeter way to spend the last moments of his life than in talking with you. I have had a dreadful night and — ah, a blessed one. It is the night that fixed my resolve, that made it firm: I will die! When I tore myself from you yesterday, in the fearful upheaval of my senses, when everything crowded in on my heart, and my hopeless, joyless being beside you took hold of me with a ghastly cold — I barely reached my room; out of my mind, I fell on my knees, and O God, you granted me the last refreshment of the bitterest tears! A thousand plans, a thousand prospects raged through my soul, and at last it stood there, one, whole, last thought: I will die! I lay down, and this morning, in the calm of waking, it stands firm, still strong in my heart: I will die. It isn't despair — it's certainty that I've carried it through, that I'm sacrificing myself for you. Yes, Charlotte, why should I hide it? One of us three must go, and I will be the one! O my dearest, in this torn heart the savage thought has crept more than once — to kill your husband! — you! — myself! — So be it, then. When you climb up the mountain on a fine summer evening, think of me then, how I so often came up the valley to you, and then look across at the churchyard to my grave, where the wind sways the tall grass to and fro in the light of the setting sun. — I was calm when I began, and now, now I weep like a child, with all this so alive around me.

Toward ten Werther called his servant and, while dressing, told him he'd be setting out on a journey in a few days; he should brush the clothes and get everything ready for packing; he also ordered him to ask for the accounts everywhere, to fetch back some borrowed books, and to pay out two months ahead to some poor people he'd been giving a weekly sum.

He had his meal brought to his room, and after it rode out to the steward's, whom he didn't find at home. He walked, deep in thought, in the garden, and seemed bent at the end on heaping up every sad memory.

The little ones didn't leave him in peace long; they chased after him, climbed on him, told him that after tomorrow, and another tomorrow, and one more day, they'd fetch their Christmas gifts at Charlotte's, and told him all the wonders their little imaginations had promised them. "Tomorrow," he cried, "and another tomorrow, and one more day!" and kissed them all warmly, and was about to go, when the little one wanted to whisper something more in his ear. He let out that his big brothers had written fine New Year's cards, so big! one for papa, one for Albert and Charlotte, and one for Werther too; they'd hand them over early on New Year's morning. That undid him; he gave them each something, mounted his horse, sent his greetings to the old man, and rode off with tears in his eyes.

Toward five he came home, told the maid to mind the fire and keep it up into the night. The servant was to pack the books and linen at the bottom of the trunk and stitch up his coats. Then it seems he wrote the following, the last paragraph of the letter to Charlotte:

You don't expect me. You think I'll obey you and not see you again before Christmas Eve. O Charlotte! today or never. On Christmas Eve you'll hold this paper in your hand, trembling, wetting it with your dear tears. I will, I must! Oh, how good it is to me, now that I've made up my mind.
Charlotte, meanwhile, had fallen into a strange state. After her last talk with Werther she'd felt how hard it would be to part from him, how he'd suffer if he had to leave her.

It had been said, more or less in passing, in front of Albert, that Werther wouldn't come again before Christmas Eve, and Albert had ridden off to a neighboring official to settle some business that would keep him overnight.

Now she sat alone; none of her brothers and sisters was near her; she gave herself up to her thoughts, which moved quietly over her situation. She saw herself bound forever to a man whose love and faithfulness she knew, to whom she was devoted with her whole heart, whose calm, whose steadiness seemed truly heaven-sent as the ground a good woman builds her life's happiness on; she felt what he would always be to her and her children. On the other side, Werther had grown so dear to her; from the very first moment of their acquaintance the harmony of their souls had shown itself so beautifully, and the long, unbroken company they'd kept, and so many shared experiences, had stamped themselves on her heart past wiping out. Everything she felt or thought worth feeling she'd grown used to sharing with him, and his going threatened to tear a gap in her whole being that couldn't be filled again. Oh, if only she could have turned him into a brother in that moment — how happy she'd have been! — if she could have married him to one of her friends, could have hoped to set things right between him and Albert too!
She ran through her friends one by one and found something against each, found none she'd have wanted to grant him.

Through all these thoughts she felt, deeply, for the first time, without making it clear to herself, that her own secret heart's wish was to keep him for herself — and at once told herself she couldn't, mustn't keep him; her pure, fine soul, so often light and able to help itself, felt the press of a sadness barred from any prospect of happiness. Her heart was crushed, and a dark cloud lay over her eyes.

It was half past six when she heard Werther coming up the stairs, and soon knew his step, his voice asking after her. How her heart beat — we might almost say for the first time — at his coming. She'd gladly have had herself denied to him, and when he came in she cried out, in a kind of passionate confusion, "You haven't kept your word!" "I promised nothing," was his answer. "Then at least you should have granted my plea," she said; "I begged it for both our sakes."

She hardly knew what she was saying, hardly what she was doing, when she sent for some friends so as not to be alone with Werther. He set down a few books he'd brought, asked after others; and now she wished her friends would come, now wished they'd stay away. The maid came back to say both were sorry, but couldn't come.

She thought of having the maid sit with her work in the next room; then changed her mind again. Werther paced the room; she went to the piano and began a minuet, but it wouldn't come right. She pulled herself together and sat down calmly beside Werther, who had taken his usual place on the sofa.

"Have you nothing to read?" she said. He had nothing. "In there in my drawer," she began, "is your translation of some of Ossian's songs; I haven't read them yet, for I always hoped to hear you read them; but it never came to that, there was never the time." He smiled, fetched the songs; a shudder went through him as he took them in his hands, and his eyes filled with tears as he looked down at them. He sat, and read:

Star of the falling night! Fair is your light in the west; you lift your shining head from your cloud, and walk in your beauty over your hill. What do you look for on the heath? The stormy winds have died. The far-off torrent murmurs. The roaring waves climb the distant rock. The flies of evening swarm on their faint wings, their humming over the field. What do you look for, fair light? But you smile and go; the waves crowd joyfully round and bathe your lovely hair. Farewell, you quiet beam. Rise, you glorious light of Ossian's soul!

And it rises in its strength. I see my departed friends; they gather on Lora, as in the years gone by. Fingal comes like a wet pillar of mist; his heroes are round him. And see, the bards of song: gray-haired Ullin! stately Ryno! Alpin, sweet singer — and you, soft-wailing Minona! How changed you are, my friends, since the days of the feast at Selma, when we vied for the honor of song, like spring breezes bending the soft grass this way and that as they pass over the hill.

Then Minona came forth in her beauty, eyes downcast, full of tears; her hair blew heavy in the gusts that came in fits off the hill. The heroes' souls grew dark when she lifted the lovely voice; for often they had seen the grave of Salgar, often the dark house of white-breasted Colma. Colma, left alone on the hill, her tuneful voice! Salgar had promised to come; but night fell around her. Hear the voice of Colma, sitting alone on the hill!
Colma. It is night! I am alone, lost on the hill of storms. The wind howls on the mountain. The torrent roars down the cliff. No hut shelters me from the rain — forsaken on the hill of winds.

Come out, moon, from behind your clouds! Show yourselves, stars of the night! Let some light lead me to the place where my love rests from the labor of the hunt — his slack bow beside him, his dogs panting around him. But here I must sit alone on the rock by the mossy stream. The stream and the wind roar; I can't hear my love's voice! Why does my Salgar wait? Has he forgotten his word? Here is the rock, and the tree, and the rushing stream! You promised to be here at nightfall. Ah, where has my Salgar gone? With you I'd flee my father, with you my proud brother. Our houses have long been enemies — but we are not enemies, O Salgar!

Be still a while, O wind! Be quiet a moment, O stream, that my voice may sound through the valley, that my wanderer may hear me! Salgar! It is I who call. Here is the tree, and the rock. Salgar! my love! I am here. Why do you wait so long to come? See, the moon shows herself, the flood gleams in the valley, the rocks stand gray on the hill — but I don't see him on the height, his dogs don't run ahead to tell me he's near. Here I must sit alone.

But who are these lying below on the heath? My love? My brother? Speak, O my friends! They do not answer. How my soul is racked with dread! Ah, they are dead! Their swords red from the fight. O my brother, my brother, why have you struck down my Salgar? O my Salgar, why have you struck down my brother? You were both dear to me! What can I say in your praise? Beautiful you were on the hill among thousands; he was terrible in battle. Speak to me! Hear my voice, sons of my love! But ah, they are silent, silent forever! Cold as the earth their breasts! Oh, from the rock on the hill, from the top of the storm-blown height, speak, ghosts of the dead! Speak — I will not be afraid! Where have you gone to rest? In what cleft of the hills shall I find you? I hear no faint voice in the wind, no answer half-drowned in the storms of the hill.

I sit in my grief; I wait, weeping, for the morning. Dig the grave, you friends of the dead, but don't close it till I come. My life flees like a dream — how should I stay behind? Here I'll rest with my friends, by the stream of the sounding rock. When night comes on the hill, when the wind rises over the heath, my ghost will stand in the wind and mourn the death of my friends. The hunter will hear me from his shelter, will dread and love my voice; for sweet shall my lament be for my friends — both were dear to me!

That was your song, Minona, soft-blushing daughter of Torman. Our tears fell for Colma, and our souls grew dark. Then Ullin came with the harp and gave us Alpin's song. Alpin's voice was kind, Ryno's soul a beam of fire; but already they rested in the narrow house, and their voice had died away in Selma. Once, before the heroes fell, Ullin came back from the hunt; he heard their contest of song on the hill. Their song was soft but sad. They mourned the fall of Morar, first of men; his soul was like Fingal's soul, his sword like Oscar's. But he fell, and his father wailed, and his sister's eyes were full of tears — Minona's eyes, the sister of the great Morar. She drew back before Ullin's song, as the moon in the west draws back when she feels the storm coming and hides her lovely head in a cloud. I struck the harp with Ullin, for the song of mourning.

Ryno. The wind and the rain are gone; the noon is bright; the clouds part. Fleeting, the sun lights the hill as it passes. Red the mountain stream runs down the valley. Sweet is your murmur, stream — but sweeter the voice I hear. It is Alpin's voice, the son of song, mourning the dead. His head is bowed with age, his weeping eye red. Alpin, glorious singer, why are you alone on the silent hill? Why do you wail, like a gust in the wood, like a wave on the far-off shore?

Alpin. My tears, Ryno, are for the dead; my voice for those who lie in the grave. Tall you are on the hill, fair among the sons of the heath — but you too will fall like Morar, and the mourner will sit on your grave. The hills will forget you; your bow will lie slack in the hall.

You were swift, O Morar, as a deer on the heath, terrible as the fire of the night-lights in heaven. Your wrath was a storm; your sword in battle, lightning over the field. Your voice was like the woodland stream after rain, like thunder on far hills. Many fell by your arm, the flame of your fury ate them up. But when you came home from war, how peaceful your brow! Your face was like the sun after the storm, like the moon in the still night; your breast calm as the lake when the howling wind has lain down.

Narrow is your dwelling now, dark your home! With three strides I measure your grave, O you who were once so great! Four stones, moss on their heads, are all that's left of you; a leafless tree, tall grass whistling in the wind, show the hunter's eye the grave of the mighty Morar. No mother is left to weep for you, no girl with the tears of love. Dead is she who bore you; fallen the daughter of Morglan.

Who comes leaning on his staff? Who is this, his head white with age, his eyes red with weeping? It is your father, O Morar, the father of no son but you. He heard of your fame in battle, heard of enemies scattered; he heard Morar's glory — ah, why did he hear nothing of your wound? Weep, father of Morar, weep! But your son does not hear you. Deep is the sleep of the dead, low their pillow of dust. Never again will he heed your voice, never wake at your call. When will it be morning in the grave, to tell the sleeper: wake! Farewell, noblest of men, you conqueror on the field! But the field will see you no more; the dark wood will never again gleam with the light of your sword. You left no son, but the song shall keep your name. Days to come shall hear of you, hear of the fallen Morar.

Loud was the grief of all, but loudest the broken sigh of Armin. It called back the death of his son, fallen in his young days. Carmor sat near the hero, the chief of the sounding Galmal. "Why does Armin sob so?" he said. "What is there here to weep for? Doesn't song ring out, and music, to melt and gladden the soul? It is like the soft mist that rises from the lake and spreads over the valley, so that the flowers fill with dew; but the sun comes back in its strength, and the mist is gone. Why so cast down, Armin, lord of sea-girt Gorma?"

Cast down? Indeed I am, and not without cause for grief. Carmor, you have lost no son, you have lost no blooming daughter. Colgar the brave lives, and Annira, fairest of maidens. The branches of your house flourish, O Carmor; but Armin is the last of his line. Dark is your bed, Daura, and heavy your sleep in the grave. When will you wake again with your songs, with your sweet voice?

Rise, you winds of autumn, rise! Storm over the dark heath! Roar, you streams of the woods! Howl, you tempests, in the crowns of the oaks! Stride, O moon, through the broken clouds, and let your pale face shine out now and then! Bring back to me the night of horror when all my children fell — when Arindal the strong fell, when Daura the lovely passed away. Daura, my daughter, you were beautiful, fair as the moon on the hills of Fura, white as fallen snow, sweet as the breathing air! Arindal, your bow was strong, your spear swift in the field, your look like mist on the wave, your shield a red cloud in the storm. Armar, famed in war, came and sought Daura's love; she did not long refuse, and fair were their friends' hopes.

But Erath, Odgal's son, raged, for his brother had fallen by Armar's hand. He came disguised as a boatman; fair was his skiff on the wave, white his hair with age, calm his grave face. "Loveliest of girls," he said, "fair daughter of Armin! Out on the sea, not far, a rock bears a tree, its red fruit shining from afar. There Armar waits for Daura; I am come to bring his love across the rolling sea." She went with him; she called for Armar — and nothing answered but the voice of the rock. "Armar! my love! my love! why do you torment me so with fear? Hear me, son of Arnart, hear! It is Daura who calls you!" Erath, the traitor, fled to land, laughing. She lifted her voice, called for her father, her brother: "Arindal! Armin! Is there none to save your Daura?"

Her voice came over the sea. Arindal, my son, came down from the hill, wild with the spoils of the hunt, his arrows rattling at his side, his bow in his hand, five dark-gray dogs at his heel. He saw bold Erath on the shore, seized him and bound him to an oak, wound the thongs hard about his hips; the captive filled the wind with his groans. Arindal pushed out over the waves in his boat to bring Daura back. Then Armar came in his fury and loosed the gray-feathered arrow. It sang, it sank into your heart, O Arindal, my son! You died in the traitor Erath's place. The oar stopped at the rock; he sank down on it and gave up his breath. What was your grief, O Daura, when your brother's blood ran at your feet! The boat was smashed. Armar threw himself into the sea to save his Daura, or to die; but a gust off the hill swept down on the waves, and he sank and rose no more.

Alone on the wave-beaten rock I heard my daughter wail. Many and loud were her cries, and her father could not save her. All night I stood on the shore; I saw her in the faint moonlight, all night I heard her cry; loud was the wind, and the rain beat hard on the side of the hill. Her voice grew faint before the morning came; it died away like the evening wind in the grass of the rocks. Heavy with grief she died, and left you, Armin, alone. Gone is my strength in war, fallen my pride among women. When the storms come down from the hills, when the north wind lifts the waves, I sit on the sounding shore and look across at the dreadful rock.
Often, by the setting moon, I see the ghosts of my children; half-seen, they walk together in their mournful talk.

A stream of tears that broke from Charlotte's eyes and gave her crushed heart air put a stop to Werther's reading. He flung down the songs, took her hand, and wept the bitterest tears. Charlotte leaned on her other hand and hid her eyes in her handkerchief. Both were in a fearful state. They felt their own misery in the fate of the noble ones, felt it together, and their tears flowed as one. Werther's lips and eyes burned against Charlotte's arm; a shudder seized her; she wanted to go, and pain and pity lay over her like lead, numbing her. She breathed, to come to herself, and begged him, sobbing, to go on — begged it in a voice straight from heaven. Werther shook, his heart fit to break; he took up the page again and read, his voice half-broken:

Why do you wake me, breath of spring? You coax me and say: I sprinkle you with the dew of heaven! But the time of my withering is near, near the storm that will strike down my leaves. Tomorrow the wanderer will come, will come, who saw me in my beauty; his eye will look about the field for me and will not find me.

The full force of these words fell on the unhappy man. He threw himself down before Charlotte in utter despair, seized her hands, pressed them to his eyes, to his forehead, and it seemed to flash through her soul, a foreboding of his terrible plan. Her senses reeled; she pressed his hands, pressed them to her breast, bent toward him with a sorrowful tenderness, and their burning cheeks touched. The world was lost to them. He threw his arms around her, crushed her to his breast, and smothered her trembling, stammering lips with furious kisses. "Werther!" she cried in a choked voice, turning away — "Werther!" and with a weak hand pushed his breast from hers; "Werther!" she cried, in the steady tone of the noblest feeling. He did not resist; he let her go from his arms and threw himself, out of his mind, down before her. She tore herself up, and in anxious confusion, trembling between love and anger, she said, "That was the last time! Werther, you will not see me again." And with a look full of love at the wretched man, she rushed into the next room and locked the door behind her. Werther stretched his arms after her, but didn't dare hold her back. He lay on the floor, his head on the sofa, and stayed so for more than half an hour, until a noise brought him to himself. It was the maid, come to lay the table. He paced the room, and when he was alone again he went to the door of the side room and called softly: "Charlotte! Charlotte! just one more word! a farewell!" She said nothing. He waited, and begged, and waited. Then he tore himself away and cried, "Farewell, Charlotte! Farewell forever!"

He came to the town gate. The watchmen, who knew him, let him out without a word. Snow and sleet were falling; only toward eleven did he knock again at his door. His servant noticed, when Werther came into the house, that his master had lost his hat. He didn't dare say anything; he helped him off with his things, which were soaked through. His hat was found later on a cliff, looking down into the valley off the slope of the hill; it's past understanding how he climbed it, on a wet, dark night, without falling to his death.
He lay down in bed and slept long. The servant found him writing when he brought the coffee next morning at his call. He was writing the following, to Charlotte:

For the last time, then, the last, I open these eyes. They will, alas, see the sun no more; a dull, misty day keeps it hidden. So mourn, Nature! Your son, your friend, your love is near his end. Charlotte, this is a feeling like no other, and yet it comes closest to a dim dream when one says to oneself: this is the last morning. The last! Charlotte, I have no sense for that word — the last! Don't I stand here now in all my strength, and tomorrow lie stretched out and slack on the ground? To die! What does that mean? See, we dream when we speak of death. I have seen many a man die; but our nature is so narrow that it has no sense of the beginning and the end of its existence. Now still mine — yours! yours, beloved! And in a moment — parted, sundered — perhaps forever? — No, Charlotte, no. How can I pass away, how can you pass away? We are, after all! Pass away — what does that mean? It's only a word, an empty sound, that nothing in my heart can feel. Dead, Charlotte! shut into the cold ground, so close, so dark! — I had a friend who was everything to my helpless youth; she died, and I followed her body, and stood by the grave as they let the coffin down and drew the ropes whirring out from under it, and the first spadeful of earth fell and the frightened box gave back a dull sound, duller and duller, and at last was covered over! I fell down by the grave — shaken, gripped, terrified, my inmost heart torn open — but I knew nothing of what was happening to me, what would happen to me. To die! the grave! I don't understand the words! Oh, forgive me! forgive me! Yesterday — it should have been the last moment of my life. O you angel! For the first time, the first, without the least doubt, it burned through my inmost being: she loves me, she loves me! Still the holy fire burns on my lips, that streamed from yours; a new, warm bliss is in my heart. Forgive me! forgive me!

Ah, I knew you loved me, knew it from the first soulful look, from the first clasp of your hand; and yet, when I was away from you again, when I saw Albert at your side, I sank again into feverish doubts.

Do you remember the flowers you sent me when, at that hateful party, you could neither give me a word nor your hand? Oh, half the night I was on my knees before them, and they sealed your love to me. But ah, those impressions passed, as the feeling of his God's grace slowly fades from the heart of the believer, given to him in full heavenly fullness through holy and visible signs.

All that passes; but no eternity shall put out the burning life I drank yesterday from your lips, that I feel within me! She loves me! This arm has held her, these lips have trembled on hers, this mouth has stammered against mine. She is mine! You are mine! Yes, Charlotte, forever.

And what does it mean, that Albert is your husband? Husband! That would be for this world, then — and for this world a sin, that I love you, that I'd like to tear you out of his arms into mine? Sin? Good — and I punish myself for it; I've tasted it in its whole heavenly bliss, this sin, drawn balm of life and strength into my heart. From this hour you are mine! mine, O Charlotte! I go ahead! I go to my Father, to your Father. To him I'll make my plaint, and he'll comfort me until you come — and I'll fly to meet you and seize you and stay with you, before the face of the Infinite, in an endless embrace.

I'm not dreaming, not raving! So near the grave, it grows light to me. We shall be! We shall see each other again! See your mother! I'll see her, find her, ah, and pour out my whole heart before her — your mother, your very likeness.
Toward eleven Werther asked his servant whether Albert had come home. The servant said yes, he'd seen his horse led out. At that the master gave him an open note that ran:
Would you lend me your pistols for a journey I have ahead of me? Keep well!

The dear woman had slept little that night; what she'd dreaded was decided, decided in a way she could neither have foreseen nor feared. Her blood, that had always flowed so pure and light, was in a feverish uproar; a thousand feelings tore at her fine heart. Was it the fire of Werther's embraces she felt in her breast? Was it anger at his boldness? Was it a sullen comparing of her present state with those days of wholly free, untroubled innocence and easy trust in herself? How was she to meet her husband, how confess to him a scene she might well confess, and yet didn't dare? They'd kept silent so long with each other — and should she be the first to break it, and at just the wrong moment make her husband so unwelcome a discovery? Already she feared that the mere news of Werther's visit would strike him badly, and now this unlooked-for catastrophe on top of it! Could she really hope her husband would see her in the right light, take it without the least prejudice? And could she wish he should read in her soul? And yet again, could she dissemble before the man to whom she'd always stood as open and clear as glass, from whom she'd never hidden, never could hide, a single feeling? Each thought troubled her, set her at a loss; and again and again her mind came back to Werther, lost to her, whom she couldn't let go, whom — alas — she had to leave to himself, and for whom, once he'd lost her, nothing was left.

How heavily the deadlock lay on her now — the thing that had settled between her and Albert, which she couldn't even now explain to herself! Such sensible, such good people had begun, over secret differences, to fall silent toward each other, each brooding on his own right and the other's wrong, and the matter so tangled and inflamed that the knot, just at the critical moment when everything hung on it, was impossible to loose. Had a happy openness brought them together sooner again, had love and forbearance come alive between them and opened their hearts, perhaps our friend might still have been saved.

There was one more strange thing in it. Werther had never made a secret, as we know from his letters, that he longed to leave this world. Albert had often argued against it, and Charlotte and her husband had sometimes spoken of it together. He, with his decided dislike of the act itself, had often shown, with a kind of touchiness quite unlike him, that he found great cause to doubt the seriousness of such a purpose; he'd even made a joke of it now and then, and passed his unbelief on to Charlotte. This eased her heart when her thoughts turned to the sad picture, but on the other hand it kept her from sharing with her husband the fears that tormented her just then.

Albert came home, and Charlotte went to meet him with a hurried embarrassment; he was out of humor, his business unfinished; the neighboring official had shown himself a stubborn, narrow man. The bad road, too, had soured him on the way.

He asked whether anything had happened, and she answered too quickly that Werther had been there the evening before. He asked whether any letters had come, and was told a letter and some packages lay in his room. He went in, and Charlotte was left alone.

The presence of the man she loved and honored had made a new impression on her heart. The memory of his nobility, his love, his good nature had calmed her soul more; she felt a secret pull to follow him, took up her work and went into his room, as she so often did. She found him busy breaking the seals and reading. Some of the contents seemed less than pleasant. She asked a few questions; he answered shortly and went to his desk to write.

They were together that way for an hour, and Charlotte's mood grew darker and darker. She felt how hard it would be to make clear to her husband, even in the best of moods, what lay on her heart; and she sank into a sadness all the more frightening because she tried to hide it and to swallow her tears.

The appearance of Werther's boy threw her into the greatest distress. He handed Albert the note, and Albert turned coolly to his wife and said, "Give him the pistols." — "I wish him a good journey," he said to the boy. It struck her like a thunderbolt; she rose, swaying; she didn't know what was happening to her. Slowly she went to the wall, took down the weapons trembling, wiped the dust from them, hesitated, and would have put it off longer if Albert hadn't pressed her with a questioning look. She gave the boy the unhappy things without being able to get out a word, and when he'd gone she gathered up her work and went to her room, in a state past all telling. Her heart foretold every horror. Now she was on the point of throwing herself at her husband's feet, confessing everything, the scene of the evening before, her guilt and her forebodings. Then again she saw no good could come of it; least of all could she hope to talk her husband into going to Werther. The table was laid; a good friend, who'd only come to ask something and meant to go at once, stayed — and made the talk at table bearable; they forced themselves, chatted, told stories, forgot.
The boy brought the pistols to Werther, who took them in raptures when he heard Charlotte had handed them over herself. He had bread and wine brought, sent the boy off to eat, and sat down to write:

They've come through your hands, you wiped the dust off them, I kiss them a thousand times, you touched them; and you, spirit of heaven, favor my resolve! And you, Charlotte, hand me the instrument, you from whose hands I wished to take my death, and ah, now do. Oh, I questioned my boy. You trembled as you gave them to him; you said no farewell! Woe, woe! no farewell? Should you have closed your heart to me for that moment that bound me to you forever? Charlotte, no age can blot it out! And I feel it — you cannot hate the man who burns so for you.

After the meal he had the boy finish packing, tore up many papers, went out and settled some small debts. He came home again, went out once more past the gate into the country despite the rain, into the count's garden, roamed farther about the neighborhood, and came back as night fell, and wrote:

Wilhelm, I have seen field and wood and sky for the last time. Farewell to you too! Dear mother, forgive me! Comfort her, Wilhelm! God bless you both! All my affairs are in order. Farewell! We shall see each other again, and more gladly.

I've paid you ill, Albert, and you forgive me. I broke the peace of your house; I brought distrust between you. Farewell! I mean to end it. Oh, that my death might make you happy! Albert! Albert! make that angel happy! And so may God's blessing rest on you!

He spent the evening still rummaging among his papers; he tore up a great deal and threw it into the stove, sealed a few packets addressed to Wilhelm. They held short essays, scattered thoughts, several of which I've seen. At ten he had the fire built up and a bottle of wine brought, and sent the servant — whose room, like the rest of the household's, lay far off at the back — to bed. The man lay down in his clothes, to be ready early, for his master had said the post-horses would be at the door before six.

Past eleven. All is so still around me, and my soul is so calm. I thank you, God, who give these last moments such warmth, such strength. I go to the window, my dearest, and see, and still see, through the storm-clouds flying past, a few stars of the everlasting sky! No, you will not fall! The Eternal carries you on his heart, and me. I see the shaft-stars of the Wagon, dearest of all the constellations. When I left you at night and stepped out your gate, it stood facing me. With what drunkenness I've often looked at it! Often, with raised hands, made it the sign, the holy marker of my present bliss! and still — O Charlotte, what doesn't bring you back to me? Aren't you all around me? and haven't I, like a child, never had enough, snatching up the little things you, dear saint, had touched?
Dear silhouette! I leave it back to you, Charlotte, and beg you to keep it sacred. A thousand, a thousand kisses I've pressed on it, a thousand greetings I've waved to it, coming and going.

I've asked your father in a note to look after my body. In the churchyard are two linden trees, back in the corner toward the field; there I want to rest. He can, he will, do this for his friend. Ask him too. I won't expect pious Christians to lay their bodies beside a poor unhappy man. Ah, I wish you'd bury me by the wayside, or in a lonely valley, where priest and Levite would pass the marked stone and bless themselves, and the Samaritan would shed a tear.

See, Charlotte! I don't shudder to take the cold, dreadful cup from which I'll drink the dizziness of death. You handed it to me, and I don't waver. All, all the wishes and hopes of my life — fulfilled! So cold, so stiff, to knock at the brass door of death. — That I might have had the happiness to die for you! Charlotte, to give myself for you! I'd die bravely, I'd die gladly, if I could give you back the peace, the joy of your life. But ah, it was given only to a few noble souls to shed their blood for their people, and through their death to fan a new, hundredfold life for their friends.

I want to be buried in these clothes, Charlotte; you touched them, made them holy. I've asked your father for this too. My soul hovers over the coffin. Let no one search my pockets. This pink bow you wore at your breast the first time I found you among your children — oh, kiss them a thousand times and tell them the fate of their unhappy friend. The dear ones! they swarm around me. Ah, how I bound myself to you! From the first moment I couldn't let you go! — This bow shall be buried with me. You gave it to me on my birthday. How I devoured it all! Ah, I never thought the road would lead me here. Be calm! I beg you, be calm!
They're loaded — the clock strikes twelve. So be it, then! Charlotte! Charlotte, farewell! Farewell!
A neighbor saw the flash of powder and heard the shot; but as everything stayed quiet, he thought no more of it.

In the morning at six the servant came in with a light. He found his master on the floor, the pistol, and blood. He called out, took hold of him; no answer, only a rattle still in his throat. He ran for the doctors, for Albert. Charlotte heard the bell pulled; a shiver ran through all her limbs. She woke her husband; they got up; the servant, sobbing and stammering, brought the news; Charlotte fell senseless at Albert's feet.

When the doctor reached the unhappy man, he found him past saving on the floor; the pulse still beat, the limbs were all numb. He'd shot himself through the head above the right eye; the brain was driven out. A vein was opened in his arm, for good measure; the blood ran; he still drew breath.

From the blood on the back of the chair one could tell he'd done the deed sitting at his desk; then he'd slid down and rolled convulsing about the chair. He lay against the window, drained, on his back, fully dressed, in boots, in the blue coat and the yellow waistcoat.

The house, the neighborhood, the town were in an uproar. Albert came in. They'd laid Werther on the bed, his forehead bound; his face already a dead man's, no limb stirring. The lungs still rattled, fearfully, now weak, now stronger; they waited for the end.
He'd drunk only one glass of the wine. Emilia Galotti lay open on his desk.
Of Albert's shock, of Charlotte's grief, let me say nothing.

The old steward came tearing up at the news; he kissed the dying man amid the hottest tears. His eldest sons came soon after him on foot; they fell at the bedside in helpless grief and kissed his hands and his mouth, and the eldest, whom he'd always loved most, hung on his lips until he was gone and the boy had to be dragged away by force. At noon he died. The steward's presence, and the measures he took, hushed any disturbance. That night, toward eleven, he had the body buried in the place Werther had chosen for himself.
The steward and his sons followed the body to the grave; Albert couldn't. Charlotte's life was feared for. Laborers carried him. No priest attended.
